newsitem.title: USA: BOXING-LEWIS CAMP REFUSES TO BELIEVE MCCALL IS WASHED UP.
newsitem.headline: BOXING-LEWIS CAMP REFUSES TO BELIEVE MCCALL IS WASHED UP.

text.p: This time around Lennox Lewis and his people refuse to believe Oliver McCall is just a washed up drug addict whose major accomplishment on Friday will be finding the ring.

Lewis's trainer, Frank Maloney, said Tuesday McCall's ongoing drug rehabilitation programme would not lull Lewis into thinking Friday's fight for the vacant World Boxing Council heavyweight title will be easy.

The 31-year-old McCall's legal and drug-related problems have been widely reported. However, Maloney said, "we were told the same thing in the first fight, but it turned out that he was locked up in training camp training.

"I wouldn't say we were suckered, but unfortunately Pepe (Correa, Lewis's now dismissed trainer) was listening to the rumours and kept telling us that all we were fighting was a drug addict and a sparing partner. This time Lennox is giving Oliver McCall the respect he deserves as a former heavyweight champion."
While Maloney talked of respect for McCall, Lewis has been saying he will retire if McCall beats him. If he truly thought McCall a worthwhile opponent, Lewis likely would not say that.

McCall (28-6) took the WBC title from Lewis when he knocked him silly in the second round on September 24, 1994. The Briton missed a right hand and amateurishly left himself wide open for a McCall counter right flush on the side of his head. Lewis got up but was very wobbly and the referee stopped the fight.

"There's been no corners cut for this fight in (Lewis's) training," Maloney declared. "So if it goes wrong on the night it can only go wrong because Oliver McCall is a better fighter, which I don't believe, by the way."
In addition to not taking his opponent lightly, Maloney says Lewis, 31, has matured and "learned to handle everything" that goes along with fighting in the big time.
"When he won the world championship you think, 'well that's it.' I believe he got it maybe a little too soon," Maloney said.
According to the Lewis camp, their fighter could not have hooked up with highly-regarded trainer Emanuel Steward soon enough.

Steward, who trained McCall when he fought Lewis last time, has been working on improving Lewis's notoriously bad balance and helping him to develop a game plan that does not rely only on a big right hand.
Steward said Lewis (29-1) is working on developing a varied attack, including different types of hooks, an uppercut and body movement.

Maloney said Lewis had little respect for Correa towards the end of his term as the fighter's trainer, suggesting that one of the factors that hurt the relationship was Correa's almost slavish devotion to complimenting Lewis, who knew he could not be doing everything right.
The Lewis camp believed Correa was just trying to ingratiate himself to everyone to keep his job.
"(Lewis and Steward) have an understanding," Maloney said.
"They can communicate together. That was missing before and they have a mutual respect that wasn't there before."
